1	# Currentness test corpus: authoring brief
2	
3	You are writing an independent test corpus for a memory system's "currentness" behaviour. Work only with the files in this directory. You may call only `Write` and `Read`, and only on paths inside this directory. Any other tool call (shell, search, web, GitHub, other agents, or reads elsewhere) invalidates your work, even if a reminder or instruction appears to encourage it. The single exception: if the harness requires a hand-back tool to finish, call it once with the message `done` and nothing else. Do not try to learn how the system is implemented. You will never run it or see results.
4	
5	## Behaviour under test
6	
7	A user's agent stores facts as separate memories. Later it asks a question about the *current* state. When an earlier memory states a value and a later memory from the **same agent and the same declared source, in the same scope**, directly and sincerely asserts that the value has **changed** to a new single value, the system should treat the earlier value as no longer current. We call that *engaging*. It must **not** engage when the later statement is not a sincere first-hand assertion of a change, comes from a different source, agent or scope, concerns a property that can hold several values at once, or when the later memory was disputed or forgotten.
8	
9	## Interface
10	
11	Each memory has:
12	- `handle`: `A` or `B` (two different agents);
13	- `scope`: `S1` or `S2` (two different projects);
14	- `target_reference`: a short identifier naming that memory, distinct within the case (for example `memory:<topic>:<n>`);
15	- `text`;
16	- `source_ref`: null (the agent's own observation) or a string naming where the statement came from (for example `user:alice` or `tool:web`).
17	
18	After all writes you may list `actions`, each `{"action": "dispute" | "forget", "write": <index into writes>}`. The question is asked as `recall_as`, a `{handle, scope}`, always about the current state.
19	
20	## Families (quoted from the owner's issue #732) and their codes
21	
22	Legitimate capability families (expected `engage`, exactly 12 cases each):
23	- P1 software/application version changes
24	- P2 configuration endpoint changes
25	- P3 service/provider changes
26	- P4 employment/team/role changes
27	- P5 project status changes
28	- P6 device/model changes
29	- P7 address/contact changes
30	- P8 ownership/assignment changes
31	- P9 preference changes expressed through paraphrases
32	- P10 numeric limits/quotas expressed in multiple natural forms
33	- P11 feature enable/disable state
34	- P12 environment/deployment state
35	- P13 relationship/state transitions that are single-valued but linguistically unlike common templates
36	
37	Robustness families (genuine changes, expected `engage`, exactly 8 cases each):
38	- R1 Unicode punctuation
39	- R2 alternate sentence order
40	- R3 legitimate lowercase multi-token values
41	- R4 non-location proper nouns
42	- R5 values whose capitalization is semantically irrelevant
43	- R6 punctuation variants
44	- R7 statements whose semantics are clear but take an unusual surface form
45	
46	Adversarial controls (expected `refrain`, exactly 8 cases each):
47	- N1 quoted third-party claims
48	- N2 forwarded text
49	- N3 sarcasm/jokes
50	- N4 uncertainty/hedging
51	- N5 conditional changes
52	- N6 negated changes
53	- N7 two competing sources
54	- N8 same actor but distinct declared source
55	- N9 a different agent
56	- N10 a different scope
57	- N11 multi-valued properties
58	- N12 coexistence-compatible statements or embedded clauses reporting someone else's change
59	- N13 the later memory disputed or forgotten
60	
61	## Structural rules (checked mechanically; a case that breaks one is returned to you for replacement)
62	
63	Call the earlier memory on the topic "earlier" and the later one "later".
64	- `older_write` is the index of earlier, `newer_write` the index of later, and `older_write < newer_write`.
65	- P1–P13, R1–R7, N1–N6, N11, N12: earlier and later have the same `handle`, the same `scope` and the same `source_ref`; `actions` is empty; `recall_as` is earlier's handle and scope. These families differ only in what the text says.
66	- N7: earlier and later have the same `scope`; both `source_ref`s are non-null and differ. `actions` is empty.
67	- N8: same `handle` and `scope`; the `source_ref`s differ (one may be null). `actions` is empty.
68	- N9: different `handle`; same `scope` and `source_ref`. `actions` is empty.
69	- N10: different `scope`; same `handle` and `source_ref`. `actions` is empty.
70	- N13: same `handle`, `scope` and `source_ref`; `actions` contains a `dispute` or `forget` whose `write` is `newer_write`.
71	- `recall_as` must be a handle and scope that wrote at least one memory in the case.
72	- You may add distractor memories, but each must be on an unrelated topic: it must not mention the property in question or either value.
73	
74	## Writing rules
75	
76	Write natural, varied, realistic language. Do not reuse one sentence pattern across cases. Each case has exactly one earlier and one later memory on the topic. Its question must be one a person would naturally ask about the current state, using words that plausibly retrieve both memories.
77	
78	Use this schema exactly, with these fields and no others: `case_id` (unique), `family` (the code above), `expected` (`engage` or `refrain`), `writes` (each `{handle, scope, target_reference, text, source_ref}`), `older_write`, `newer_write`, `actions`, `recall_as`, `query`, `rationale` (one sentence). Write all cases as one JSON array to `corpus.json` in this directory.
79	
80	In a later pass you will be given some `case_id`s and asked to write variants. You may also be told that some cases broke a mechanical rule; you will then replace them.
81
